parts: Lesson 26: Selection of Textiles and Clothing — Summary

Fibre properties influence choice: length and appearance (staple fibres such as cotton, jute and wool give a rough look and get dirty easily; filament fibres such as silk, nylon and polyester give a smooth shiny look and stay clean; starch gives only a temporary smoothness), moisture absorption (cotton absorbs perspiration and keeps the skin cool, so is best for summers, undergarments and baby clothes; synthetics absorb little and are uncomfortable in summer), heat conductivity (cotton and rayon are good conductors and keep the body cool; silk and synthetics are poor conductors; wool is a very bad conductor and keeps the body warm, so is best for winter) and strength (wool, silk and rayon become weak when wet; cotton and synthetics are strong when wet and can be scrubbed; use them for daily wear; nylon is strongest and is used for parachutes and ropes; silk for occasional use). Construction: knitting gives stretch (socks, undergarments, sweaters); weaving gives smooth, firm fabric for dresses. Finishes: shrinkage-control saves buying extra cloth, waterproofing for umbrellas; an over-starched cloth hides poor quality (rub the corner: white powder means avoid).

Climate (cotton in summer, wool in winter; turbans and long robes in deserts), occasion (bright dresses for weddings; simple formal clothes for an interview; comfortable fit for routine days), age (infants: soft, light, absorbent cotton, simple to put on, front openings with snaps; school children: strong, durable, easy to launder, extra seam allowance; teenagers: fit, style and mix-and-match for variety; adults: easy-care, wrinkle-free clothes for working women; old age: light, loose, front-opening clothes with large buttons) and profession or activity (doctors and nurses in white; uniforms; sportsmen in absorbent shorts; travelling clothes dark and not crumpling; overalls, mining suits, wet suits, space suits and fireproof clothing; snug cotton in the kitchen, not hanging dupattas).

A label (paper, plastic or tag attached to a product) gives information; a marking is printed on the surface of fabric or 'thaan'. Types: brand labels (company identity), descriptive labels (size, variety), certification labels (Woolmark for pure wool), care labels (washing, ironing, storing) and informative labels (composition, performance, care and use). Malpractices: giving less quantity or poor quality (short measuring rod, stretching fabric: 4 m turns out to be 3.8 m), cheating on price (charging more than the printed price or adding taxes), selling defective goods (seconds sold as fresh) and giving false, misleading or incomplete labels. The Consumer Protection Regulation Act (1988) covers these. Be alert: watch the measuring, check the printed price, read labels and use the Act.
Judging quality of fabrics and garments

Material: pleasing to touch; durability depends on fibre, yarn strength, twist and compact construction (closely woven fabric is stronger and more serviceable). Weave: avoid long floats (they snag), test strength by tension between thumbs, filler yarns should meet the selvedge at right angles (an oblique angle means off-grain) and the weave should be uniform when held to the light. Finish: smell should be clean and not oily, dyeing even (colour rubbed off along creases means poor dye), geometric patterns meeting the selvedge at right angles, no powdery dust when rubbed (too much starch or gum hides poor quality), and dense, fine pile in velvets and towels. Ready-made garments: design (style line, shape, colour, texture), fit (shoulders, bust, waist, length; not undersized or oversized), workmanship (look at the wrong side, double and finished seams, no puckers, enough seam allowance, working fasteners and zips, well-defined collar edges, neat piping and facings), price (matches quality; high price is not always high quality) and care and maintenance (read care labels; choose minimum care; check colour fastness).
